Positive Confession
POZ-ih-tiv kun-FESH-un
noun
Modern coinage from the English positive (affirming, declaring a positive state) + confession (from Latin confiteri, to acknowledge, declare aloud). The phrase became the theological self-designation of the Word-Faith movement's teaching that spoken declarations of faith create or summon the realities they affirm. Also called “name it and claim it” or “blab it and grab it.”

Biblical Definition

Positive confession is the Word-Faith teaching that Spirit-filled believers can speak material and spiritual realities into existence by uttering faith-declarations, and conversely, that negative speech or confession of sickness and poverty produces the realities it names. Associated with E.W. Kenyon, Kenneth Hagin Sr., Kenneth Copeland, and Creflo Dollar, the doctrine holds that God created the universe by speaking it into existence, that believers are “little gods” with the same creative power, and that faith is a spiritual force activated by the spoken word. Disease, poverty, and defeat are therefore products of insufficient or negative confession; health, wealth, and victory are the birthright of every believing Christian who confesses them. The movement marshals Mark 11:23 (“whoever says to this mountain”) as its proof-text and misreads Proverbs 23:7 (“as he thinks in his heart, so is he”) as a law of mental causation. These texts, read in context, teach persevering faith in God's sovereign purposes—not a metaphysical power of the human tongue to create outcomes. James 4:13–14 directly contradicts the presumption that believers can declare their future: “you do not know what tomorrow will bring.” The confession Scripture commands is confession of Christ as Lord (Rom. 10:9), acknowledgment of sin (1 John 1:9), and testimony to God's mighty acts—none of which is a mechanism for materializing personal desires.

Origin & Era

Positive confession: the Word-Faith doctrine that spoken declarations of faith create the realities they assert; the verbal mechanism by which the movement teaches that believers obtain health, wealth, and spiritual victory.

POS'I-TIVE CON-FES'SION, noun. (20th-century coinage.) In Word-Faith theology, the practice of verbally declaring desired realities (health, prosperity, spiritual authority) as already possessed in faith, on the premise that spoken faith-declarations create or summon what they affirm.

Distinguished from biblical confession, which declares what God has done and is doing (homologia = saying the same as); positive confession teaches that the believer's words themselves are causative agents.

Rooted in E.W. Kenyon's synthesis of New Thought metaphysics with Pentecostal healing culture; popularized by Kenneth Hagin Sr. and spread globally through Copeland, Dollar, and their networks.

The doctrine's logical corollary is that sickness and poverty result from inadequate or negative confession, which shifts blame onto suffering believers and distorts the theology of the cross.

Confessional theology distinguishes the confessio fidei (confession of the faith) from positive-confession practice; the former is public acknowledgment of revealed doctrine, the latter is a metaphysical claim about the causal power of speech.

Key Scripture

Mark 11:23 — ""Truly I tell you, if anyone says to this mountain, 'Go, throw yourself into the sea,' and does not doubt in their heart but believes that what they say will happen, it will be done for them."

James 4:13 — "Now listen, you who say, "Today or tomorrow we will go to this or that city, spend a year there, carry on business and make money.""

John 14:6 — "Jesus answered, "I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me."

Proverbs 23:7 — "for he is the kind of person who is always thinking about the cost. "Eat and drink," he says to you, but his heart is not with you."

Modern Corruption

Positive confession corrupts faith by relocating its object from God's sovereign grace to the believer's own verbal power, producing a theology in which God is compelled by correctly spoken formulas rather than worshipped as Lord.

expand to see more

Positive confession is not an excess of faith but a replacement of it. Biblical faith is directed toward God as He has revealed Himself—sovereign, good, and wise in all His dispensations. Positive-confession faith is directed toward one's own declarations as causative forces; God becomes the mechanism through which correctly spoken faith is honored. The result is that suffering, unanswered prayer, and persistent illness are read as failures of the believer rather than as the mysteries of divine providence, producing pastoral devastation when the formula doesn't work. Churches that tolerate positive-confession teaching inevitably produce either manipulative triumphalism or a collapse of faith among those whose “confessions” did not yield the promised results.

The recovery is the theology of the cross. Christ, on the night of His betrayal, did not confess deliverance; He said “not my will, but Yours be done” (Luke 22:42). Paul—the apostle who prayed three times about his thorn in the flesh and received not removal but the grace to bear it (2 Cor. 12:7–9)—is the New Testament's definitive answer to positive confession. God is not a force activated by verbal formulas; He is the Lord who gives and takes away, whose ways are higher than ours, and whose glory is magnified precisely in the patient faith of suffering saints.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The English compound positive + confession names a practice rooted not in Scripture but in the New Thought metaphysics of the late 19th century, dressed in Pentecostal language.

expand to see more

Latin positivus — established, settled, affirmative; in positive confession, the “positive” declaration is the mechanism of reality-creation

Latin confiteri — to confess, acknowledge, declare openly; in biblical use always directed to what God has done, not to desired outcomes

Greek homologia — saying the same thing; the NT word for confession means agreeing with God's declaration, not generating new realities by speech

New Thought metaphysics (19th c.) — the philosophical source; E.W. Kenyon synthesized its “mind over matter” framework with biblical language, producing the Word-Faith system

Greek rhema — spoken word; Word-Faith theology distinguishes rhema (the spoken, activated word) from logos (the written word) to legitimize its confessional formulas

Usage

"The pastoral damage of positive-confession teaching is most visible in cancer wards and ICUs, where dying believers are told their condition results from insufficient faith or negative confession."

"Distinguishing positive confession from the biblical practice of intercessory prayer and praise is essential: prayer addresses God and submits to His will; positive confession addresses reality and commands it."

"Word-Faith networks are embedded in many Pentecostal and charismatic streams; pastors planting or leading in these contexts must be explicit about what the biblical doctrine of faith does and does not claim."
